channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Something to be done? Get Lillian
item.description: A portrait of Lillian Frank, Melbourne's flamboyant queen of hairdressing, whose 15-year reign of spectacular fashion at the Cup, seven front pages at Hair's opening night, and newly acquired role promoting Rocky Mattioli's world title fight proves she is as far from shy as Eva Gabor.

item.title: A far cry — or yodel — from Bazza
item.description: On the set of Bruce Beresford's "The Getting of Wisdom," Barry Humphries plays a pious Presbyterian headmaster while a young Susannah Fowle takes the lead role of Laura — a world away from Bazza McKenzie, with the original PLC demolished and scenes shot at Illawarra's grand staircase.

item.title: The inversion of a wine snob
item.description: Keith Dunstan confesses his long career as a fake wine expert — from home-bottling in turpentine bottles and pillaging Toorak rubbish bins for empties, through the painful stages of wine snobbery, to his current humiliating attempt to wean himself back to the cheap stuff.

item.title: Dame Edna bares all — in limp and stiff
item.description: Dame Edna Everage arrives by Rolls-Royce with a mounted police escort and the Dandenong Marching Grannies to launch her Coffee Table Book — a guide to gracious living featuring funnel web spider cake, Norm's prostate diagram, and poems denouncing Melbourne's massage parlors.

item.title: The long march wasn't much longer
item.description: A China-watcher reports from St Kilda Road on the queues for Melbourne's Chinese exhibition, which is bigger than Blue Poles, bigger than the Modern Masters, and even bigger than King Kong — with the jade suit of Princess Tou Wan drawing reverent crowds and their irreverent commentary.

item.title: The great Australian stupor test
item.description: The Centenary Test brought magnificent cricket and magnificent crowds — but also yobs in towelling hats and thongs with eskies the size of coffins, chanting "Lill-ee, Lill-ee" whether Lillee was bowling or not, and booing brilliant cover drives by the opposition.

item.title: The wowsers still pack a solid vote
item.description: The Pizza Hut at Box Hill discovers what the district's curious dry history already knows — that Camberwell, named after a pub but gone dry in 1920, still returns its local option polls against liquor by a solid majority, even when a pizza chain spends $4000 canvassing every elector.

item.title: The final passing of the horse
item.description: Melbourne mourns the end of horse-drawn milk deliveries — the last of the 19th century in a city that once had every trade deliver by horse and cart — while a computer expert promises that within five years nobody will be delivering anything at all.

item.title: The FJ Holden is today's ideal car
item.description: Prompted by the petrol crisis and President Carter's demands for smaller cars, Keith Dunstan proposes reviving the FJ Holden — weighing seven cwt less than a modern Kingswood, capable of 34 miles to the gallon, and now acquiring a dashing romantic symbolism via a new Australian film.

item.title: The strike launched a serene cycle
item.description: The tanker strike turned Melbourne briefly into something like Amsterdam — cars banished, bicycles everywhere, the Fitzroy Gardens visible for the first time in years, 91,000 people walking to the MCG for Anzac Day, and road deaths dropping to eight — while the union chief's unlisted namesake in the phone book fielded bomb threats.

item.title: The "Old dark blue" goes pink
item.description: Melbourne Grammar announces 25 girls will start at Grimwade House next year — a momentous break for Australia's oldest Anglican public school, which has produced three Prime Ministers — while cold economics drives the co-ed trend across Victoria's private schools, with over 200 girls already at Geelong Grammar and female crews heading for the Head of the River.

item.title: A fight over faded glory
item.description: The Regent Theatre sits in comic stalemate — the Municipal Officers' Association banning its reconstruction, the Builders' Laborers banning its demolition, and costing $800,000 a year while doing nothing — with enough colourful characters to cast a perfect film about its long and tortured story.

item.title: Is nothing sacred?
item.description: The Herald reports that Moonee Valley Racing Club may go heterosexual — allowing men and women to mix in the betting rings and bars — which would cascade through Flemington, Caulfield and Sandown, ending Melbourne's cherished tradition of sexual apartheid in the members' enclosures, a curiosity as distinctive as the city's trams.

item.title: Ideas on holding down the hold-ups
item.description: Melbourne's new Tourism Authority launches amid a city famous for being the armed hold-up capital of the world — over 228 armed hold-ups this year — with the State Savings Bank's PR man cataloguing the daily public suggestions: nerve gas, marbles, trap-doors, fall-in grills, dye capsules, radio transmitters in banknotes, and the ejector seat for tellers.

item.title: Trying to sell Buckingham Palace
item.description: The ordeal of selling a family home — keeping it like Buckingham Palace in jubilee week while buyers arrive at all hours, inspect the dirty washing and criticise the kitchen, and estate agents dress it up with descriptions like "gracious Edwardian home" for a property with chip bath heater, "superb wooded garden" for morning glory holding up the garage.

item.title: Stagflation is NOT blowing up deer
item.description: On the eve of another budget, with 38 percent of economists optimistic, 28 percent predicting ruin and 34 percent waffling, Keith Dunstan offers a seminar in economic vocabulary — spiralling inflation, stagflation, buoyant or rocky outlooks, haemorrhaging reserves, and the vital concept of "viable" — so readers can hold their own at dinner parties.

item.title: We're in a parlors state
item.description: A massage parlour has opened in Keith Dunstan's South Yarra street, prompting reflection on how Melbourne has grown from 12 parlours five years ago to around 200 — the Town Planning Appeals Tribunal calls them "thinly disguised brothels" — while the Sunday Observer's four pages of advertisements offer everything from Tommy with a 48-inch bust to firelight massage and escorts for the discriminating.

item.title: My house is not, repeat not, a home
item.description: Moving out of a family home of 20 years in a single day — a chain reaction of Melbourne removalists all shifting at once — becomes an excavation through pogo sticks, hula hoops, cigarette card collections of Woodfull and Cazaly, the Guest House at Lorne photograph trick of sprinting to appear in the panoramic portrait twice, and the children's heartbreak over discarded school essays.

item.title: That dreadful regiment of joggers
item.description: The jogging and fitness craze has swept Melbourne — Lufthansa runs in-flight exercises, Prahran Market fathers arrive in matching crimson tracksuits, Toorak couples commission made-to-measure His-and-Hers wool sets at $80, and even the young attend 21sts in Adidas gear — while Keith Dunstan offers advice on the correct track-suit aesthetic, from the form-fitting leg to the ski resort badge.

item.title: Projects galore but no end in site
item.description: An adman proposes harnessing Melbourne's hot air from parliament, the City Council, the BLF and the Save the Regent Committee to power a turbine — which captures the city's crisis of confidence perfectly, as Keith Dunstan opens a form guide on its projects: Collins Place 3/1, underground 100/1, arts centre 250/1, and Newport power station at 1/1992.

item.title: Cold comfort
item.description: A letter from Trans Time Inc. of Canberra prompts a conversation with Australian agent Dr Thomas Donaldson, a mathematics lecturer at the ANU, about cryonic suspension — $50,000 for the full body, $15,000 for the head only, 28 Americans frozen so far with 14 still in thermos-bottle storage at minus 169 degrees — leading Keith Dunstan to doubt whether waking in the year 3000 would be worth the trouble.

item.title: Twice was two times too much
item.description: Melbourne endures two grand finals in a row — Channel 7's football marathon runs from midnight Friday through nine replayed finals and a champagne breakfast before the actual match draws 106,000 to the MCG — leaving wedding guests in St Raphael's Preston exchanging thumb signals about Collingwood's score during the ceremony, and brides displaced to 9 am starts so grooms can still make the game.

item.title: The colorful cloying of company reports
item.description: Annual reports in 1977 are 22.8 percent bigger than 1976, with color up 29.7 percent — EMI's features a National Geographic seascape and a gentleman wielding an electron into a cathode ray tube, Carlton and United Breweries shows a million empty pottles, BHP's board poses like a Marylebone cricket team of the 1880s, and Peter Kurts Properties labels their executives "DYNAMIC," "A LARGE YOUNG LION," and "NOT EASILY RUFFLED" in the chairman's own handwriting.

item.title: Please keep on the grass
item.description: The muesli-and-fitness revolution has overtaken Keith Dunstan's household — 5BX exercises, isometrics, Japanese cookers, vitamin E for immortality, lunchtime joggers fleeing their coronaries through the Treasury Gardens — but after mixing muesli in the bath and graduating to a plastic rubbish bin, the most remarkable result is a stomach like a five-gallon fermenting tank, and the next trend is grasses, herbs and weeds, with nasturtiums recommended to arouse the sluggish man from his torpidity.

item.title: How not to go bonkers at election time
item.description: Australia's nine legislatures have produced a federal election every second year since Federation — and with both parties spending $2 million on advertising for the current campaign — Keith Dunstan offers the Bulletin Guide to Mental Purity: avoid TV between 6 and 8.30 pm, listen to FM radio (Wagner's Siegfried is safe), throw away your letterbox junk, read newspapers from the back page, and start conversations about whether the Pope would make a good Presbyterian.

item.title: Let's get back to service with a snarl
item.description: Dunstan rails against the American import of compulsory cheerfulness — from "Have a nice day" butchers to name-tagged bank tellers — and laments the passing of the honest Australian grunt.

item.title: Melbourne's massage industry
item.description: Social welfare researcher Bronwen Rumbold lifts the lid on Melbourne's reputation as the massage parlour capital of the world, tracing the city's 300-plus parlours, their links to migration patterns and organised crime, and the Social Welfare Department's cautious attempts at reform.

item.title: Introducing the no-go road show
item.description: The F19 freeway — $87 million, five lanes each way, passing three golf courses and Fairlea women's prison — sits unused and unloved as citizen co-ordinator Andrew Herington's 800-name telephone tree triggers town hall bells and car-cadaver barricades across Alexandra Parade, while Premier Hamer finally agrees to halt work pending a new study, leaving Keith Dunstan to suggest converting it to 500 tennis courts, 300 basketball courts, or 12 drive-in theatres.

item.title: Melbourne gets behind Moomba
item.description: On its 25th anniversary, Dunstan traces the turbulent history of Moomba — from its disputed Aboriginal name meaning "let's get together and have fun" to the dramas of sinking gondolas, a cable tram wreck, Rolf Harris and the garbage strike, and Mickey Mouse's pie in the face.

item.title: Not just an ordinary, run-of-the-mill academic
item.description: A tribute to Monash University historian Ian Turner, who died on Erith Island on 27 December 1978 — former communist, carriage cleaner, jazz lover, Richmond football fanatic, and one of the most gifted lecturers Australia produced.
